section.title: The Redemption of Israel
section.sectionRationale: This chapter closes the Isaiah apocalypse, chapters 24 to 27, turning from cosmic judgment and resurrection hope to the LORD's own redemptive care for Israel, His fruitful vineyard. It opens with the LORD slaying Leviathan, the ancient serpent, and closes with scattered Israelites gathered one by one to worship on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.
section.thesis: The LORD who will finally slay Leviathan, the ancient serpent, is the same LORD who tends Israel as His own vineyard, disciplining her in measured exile rather than destroying her, atoning for her guilt, and gathering her scattered people one by one to worship Him on His holy mountain.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the LORD's sword raised against Leviathan the serpent; the song of the fruitful vineyard the LORD Himself keeps; Jacob's guilt atoned for as her idols are removed; and the great ram's horn sounding to gather Israel home for worship.

verses.text: In that day the LORD will take His sharp, great, and mighty sword, and bring judgment on {{leviathan|Leviathan}} the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the coiling serpent, and He will slay the dragon of the sea.

units.label: The song of the fruitful vineyard
units.note: the LORD Himself is its keeper

verses.text: In that day: “Sing about a fruitful vineyard.
I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually. I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it;
I am not angry. If only thorns and briers confronted Me, I would march and trample them, I would burn them to the ground.
Or let them lay claim to My protection; let them make peace with Me, yes, let them make peace with Me.”
In the days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit.
Has the LORD struck Israel as He struck her oppressors? Was she killed like those who slayed her?
By warfare and exile You contended with her and removed her with a fierce wind, as on the day the east wind blows.

Therefore Jacob's guilt will be {{kippur|atoned for}}, and the full fruit of the removal of his sin will be this: When he makes all the altar stones like crushed bits of chalk, no Asherah poles or incense altars will remain standing.
For the fortified city lies deserted, a homestead abandoned, a wilderness forsaken. There the calves graze, and there they lie down; they strip its branches bare.

When its limbs are dry, they are broken off. Women come and use them for kindling; for this is a people without understanding. Therefore their Maker has no compassion on them, and their Creator shows them no favor.

units.label: The great ram's horn gathers Israel home

verses.text: In that day the LORD will thresh from the flowing Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, and you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one.

And in that day a great ram's horn will sound, and those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt. And they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

leviathan.gloss: A great sea creature or dragon, used in the Old Testament both as a real, immense animal and as a symbol of chaos and evil opposed to God. Its final slaying by the LORD's sword anticipates the ultimate defeat of the ancient serpent, Satan, described in Revelation 12 and 20.

kippur.gloss: To atone, to cover or make reconciliation for sin, the same root behind Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Jacob's guilt being atoned for here is tied concretely to the removal of idolatry, showing that true atonement issues in a changed, purified life, not merely a cleared record.

basic.context: This chapter closes the section often called the Isaiah apocalypse with a dramatic image: the LORD slaying Leviathan, the ancient sea serpent symbolizing chaos and evil. It then shifts to gentler imagery, Israel as a fruitful vineyard the LORD Himself tends, before explaining that her painful exile was measured discipline meant to atone for her guilt and remove her idolatry, and it ends with scattered Israelites gathered home to worship on God's holy mountain.
basic.hermeneutics: The Leviathan imagery draws on ancient Near Eastern language for chaos monsters to describe God's total victory over every hostile power, historically anticipating the defeat of Israel's oppressors and, more deeply, the ultimate defeat of evil itself. The vineyard and exile material describes God's real historical discipline of Israel through Assyrian and Babylonian conquest, distinguished carefully from the total destruction He brought on her oppressors, verse 7, since His purpose for Israel was purifying atonement, not annihilation.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD's sword falls on Leviathan, a term for a great sea dragon that Scripture elsewhere uses as a picture of chaos and evil opposed to God, Job 41, Psalm 74:14. Jacob's guilt is described using kaphar, to atone, the same root behind the Day of Atonement, and here atonement is inseparable from Israel actually removing her idols, showing that true forgiveness reshapes behavior, not merely status.
basic.typology: The LORD's slaying of Leviathan anticipates Christ's decisive victory over Satan, pictured in Scripture as the ancient serpent and the dragon, begun at the cross, Colossians 2:15, and completed at His return, Revelation 20:1-10. The vineyard Israel, tended and disciplined by the LORD Himself, anticipates the true vine, Jesus, and the church grafted into Him, John 15:1-8.
basic.christ: The great sword that slays Leviathan, the ancient serpent and dragon of the sea, is fulfilled in Christ's victory over Satan, disarmed at the cross, Colossians 2:15, and finally bound and destroyed at Christ's return, Revelation 20:1-10. The atonement for Jacob's guilt, tied to the removal of idolatry, anticipates the far greater atonement Christ accomplishes, which not only covers sin but transforms hearts to actually turn from idols to serve the living God, 1 Thessalonians 1:9.
basic.god: God is both the fierce warrior who will finally destroy every power of chaos and evil, and the tender keeper of His vineyard, watering it continually and guarding it night and day. He disciplines His people in real but measured proportion, distinguishing His purifying purpose for them from His destructive judgment on their oppressors, always aiming at their atonement and restoration, not their ruin.
basic.crossReferences: Job 41:1-34 and Psalm 74:13-14 depict Leviathan as a picture of chaos that only God can subdue. Colossians 2:15 declares that Christ disarmed the powers and authorities at the cross. Revelation 20:1-10 describes the final, complete binding and destruction of the ancient serpent. John 15:1-8 develops the vineyard and vine imagery in Jesus' own teaching about abiding in Him.
basic.oneStory: This chapter moves from the LORD's promised final victory over Leviathan, the ancient serpent, through His tender, disciplined care for Israel as His vineyard, to the joyful gathering of scattered exiles to worship on His holy mountain. It anticipates the whole gospel story: Christ's decisive defeat of Satan, His atoning removal of sin's grip, and His final gathering of His people from every corner of the earth to worship Him together.

context.literary:
Chapter 27 is the last page of the Isaiah apocalypse, and it is built from four scenes that each begin with 'in that day.' The phrase opens verse 1, verse 2, verse 12 and verse 13, and it frames the chapter as a series of pictures taken from the same future morning. The scenes run from the widest scale to the smallest. Verse 1 is the cosmos, a sword against a sea monster. Verses 2 to 6 are a garden, with a keeper watering his vines. Verses 7 to 11 are a courtroom or a ledger, with questions about how severely Israel was struck and what the blow achieved. Verses 12 to 13 are a harvest and a trumpet.

The warrior and the gardener are the same person. In verse 1 the LORD takes up a sword. In verse 4 He says that if thorns and briers confronted Him He would march against them and burn them. He then turns at once to the offer of verse 5: let them claim His protection and make peace with Him. The fire is real, and so is the open door beside it.

The chapter is a deliberate answer to a song earlier in the book. Isaiah 5:1-2 sang of a beloved's vineyard on a fertile hill that produced sour grapes, and verse 6 of that song promised a wasteland of thorns and briers. Here the call is 'Sing about a fruitful vineyard,' and the thorns are now something the keeper would trample. The two songs are mirror images, with the first ending in judgment and this one ending in blossom.

The second half has a rhythm of question and answer. Verse 7 asks whether Israel was struck as her oppressors were, and verses 8 and 9 answer with a more careful measure, while verses 10 and 11 describe a deserted city whose people lacked understanding. The chapter ends not with the fruit of the vineyard but with a trumpet, so that the final sound of the apocalypse section is a gathering call.
context.historical:
The vineyard was Israel's own standing picture of herself. Psalm 80:8-9 sang of a vine uprooted from Egypt and planted in the land, and Hosea and Jeremiah accused the vine of turning to fruit for itself, Hosea 10:1, or into a rotten, wild plant, Jeremiah 2:21. Isaiah 5 had said the vineyard would be left a wasteland. By the time of Isaiah 27 the northern kingdom had fallen, 2 Kings 17:5-6, and Judah would later be carried away to Babylon, 2 Kings 25:11. The chapter's reassurance that the exile was measured would have met an audience that had seen towns emptied, fortified cities deserted and cattle grazing on the ruins, verse 10.

The Leviathan of verse 1 has an ancient Near Eastern background. A Canaanite poem from Ugarit celebrates Baal's victory over a sea monster called Lotan and gives him titles very close to the two Isaiah uses, the fleeing serpent and the twisting serpent. Scholars have long noticed the kinship. In Isaiah the borrowing is a polemic. There is no rival god and no struggle, only the LORD with His own sword, and the monster is a creature in His hand, as Psalm 104 and Genesis 1:21 would agree.

Israel's idols had names and furniture, and verse 9 mentions Asherah poles and incense altars. Hezekiah removed such things, 2 Kings 18:4, and later kings put them back. The picture of altar stones crushed like chalk describes a thorough end to a persistent habit.

The boundaries of verse 12, from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, are those of the land promised to Abraham, Genesis 15:18. Israelites in verse 13 are said to be perishing in Assyria and scattered in Egypt, a double dispersion. The northern tribes had gone to Assyria, and Judah's remnant would flee to Egypt, Jeremiah 43:5-7. The ram's horn sounded at the Jubilee, which began on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 25:9-10, a link the chapter may be using.
context.canonical:
The chapter pulls on threads from across the Bible. The sea monster appears in Job 41:1 as a creature no one can hook, in Job 3:8 as a power that cursers might wake, and in Psalm 74:13-14 as one whose heads God crushed. Job 26:13 uses the same words for the 'fleeing serpent' that Isaiah uses, and Isaiah 51:9 recalls the days when God pierced the dragon. Behind all of them stands the first serpent, whose head is to be crushed, Genesis 3:15.

The vineyard song reworks Isaiah 5, as noticed above, and sits among a family of vine texts, Psalm 80:8-9, Hosea 10:1, Jeremiah 2:21. Jesus joins this family with the parable of tenants who kill the owner's son, Matthew 21:33-43, and with His claim to be the true vine whose Father is the keeper of the vineyard, John 15:1-5. The keeper of Isaiah 27:3 is that Father.

The atonement language of verse 9 is picked up by Paul, who joins it with Isaiah 59:20-21 and writes that the Deliverer will come from Zion and remove godlessness from Jacob, 'when I take away their sins,' Romans 11:26-27. The BSB footnote on Isaiah 27:9 notes that the Greek reads that way and that Paul cites it.

The gathering and the great ram's horn are echoed by Isaiah 11:11-12, where the Lord recovers a remnant from Assyria and Egypt among other places, and by Isaiah 19:23-25, where Egypt and Assyria are blessed alongside Israel. The New Testament uses the trumpet for the gathering of the elect, Matthew 24:31, and for the raising of the dead, 1 Corinthians 15:52. Finally, Revelation takes the sea monster as the ancient serpent and describes his binding and end, Revelation 12:9, 20:2 and 20:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet wanted a scattered people to know three things. First, no power is too large for God, however primeval it sounds. The sea monster was the figure of everything that could not be tamed, and one verse is enough to dispose of it. The people did not have to fear whatever was behind the empires that had crushed them.

Second, they were to read their suffering rightly. The questions of verse 7 are the sort that people ask in exile: has God treated us as He treated our enemies? The answer is no, and the difference is the point. Their enemies were struck down, while Israel was driven away by measured blows, so that sin might be removed and the idols destroyed. The purpose of the discipline was a vineyard, not a graveyard. At the same time, verses 10 and 11 refuse to flatter them. A city that lacked understanding found no pity from its Maker, and the author wants that sobriety to sit beside the comfort.

Third, they were to look to a gathering. The fruitful vineyard and the great ram's horn are promises that the scattered would be found one by one and brought to worship on the holy mountain. Hearers who had been told by exile that they were forgotten were meant to hear a trumpet that remembered each of them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter describes what God did and will do with Israel. It does not tell every sufferer that their hardship is a stage in atonement, and the whole Bible resists that move. When disciples asked whether a man's blindness was due to sin, Jesus said it was not, John 9:2-3. The principle the chapter does give, that God's discipline of His own is measured and aims at removing sin, should not be turned into a diagnosis of any particular pain.

The chapter has one imperative, 'Sing about a fruitful vineyard,' verse 2, and one open invitation in verse 5, to let the thorns claim God's protection and make peace with Him. Those are the parts that carry directly into present life: singing about what God will do before it is visible, and treating peace with God as available to anyone who comes. The Leviathan verse should not be read as a licence to name any particular person or nation as the monster. The New Testament's own link is to Satan, Revelation 12:9, not to a human enemy.

debates.question: Is Leviathan in verse 1 a literal sea creature, a symbol of a specific historical enemy empire, or a symbol of Satan and cosmic evil generally?

views.label: A symbol of specific historical empires, such as Egypt or Babylon
views.case: Elsewhere in Scripture, similar dragon or sea monster imagery, such as Rahab, symbolizes specific oppressive empires, particularly Egypt, suggesting Leviathan here may represent a specific historical power opposed to God's people.

views.label: A symbol of cosmic evil and chaos itself, ultimately Satan
views.case: The threefold description, fleeing serpent, coiling serpent, dragon of the sea, echoes ancient Near Eastern chaos-monster imagery used elsewhere for evil in its most cosmic sense, and Revelation later applies nearly identical language directly to Satan, the ancient serpent, suggesting this verse's ultimate referent is cosmic evil rather than one historical empire alone.

debates.bearing: The two readings need not be exclusive; specific historical empires embodying chaos and opposition to God's rule can themselves be seen as manifestations of the deeper cosmic evil that Revelation identifies as Satan, so that the ultimate, final fulfillment of this verse is Christ's complete victory over the ancient serpent himself.

debates.question: What does 'Therefore Jacob's guilt will be atoned for' in verse 9 mean: does the exile itself atone, or does something else?

views.label: The exile and the destruction of idols is the means by which sin is purged
views.case: The verse reads 'Therefore,' tying atonement to the discipline of verses 7 and 8, and then names its result: altar stones crushed, no Asherah poles left standing. On this reading the suffering and the cleansing of Israel's worship are themselves the removal of sin, a purifying judgment on the nation.

views.label: The exile prepares for an atonement that God Himself provides
views.case: The verb is the one used of the Day of Atonement, and no sacrifice is mentioned here. Paul cites the verse together with a promise that the Deliverer will take away sins, Romans 11:26-27, and the New Testament teaches that sin is dealt with by the sacrifice of Christ, Hebrews 9:26. On this reading the exile clears the ground, but it cannot itself pay for guilt.

debates.bearing: Both views see the discipline as aimed at removal of sin and idols, and neither makes suffering a payment that earns forgiveness. The New Testament settles the final source of atonement in Christ, and the chapter's own emphasis falls on the fruit that follows when the idols are gone.

debates.question: What is the gathering of verses 12 and 13?

views.label: The return from exile
views.case: Israelites are said to be perishing in Assyria and scattered in Egypt, and the boundaries are those of the old land. The return of Jews to Judah under Persian rule is a first, partial answer, and later prophets speak of it in similar language.

views.label: An end-time gathering, including Gentiles and the church
views.case: The scale of the language, the great trumpet and the thresh from the Euphrates to Egypt, goes beyond the return that followed the exile, and the New Testament uses the trumpet and the gathering for the end of the age, Matthew 24:31, and for the scattered children of God gathered into one, John 11:52.

debates.bearing: Prophecy of this kind often has a near answer and a far one. The first return was real, and the New Testament reads the trumpet as still to be fully heard, with a people gathered from every direction around the One they worship.

study.originalLanguages:
The three names in verse 1 repay a closer look. Leviathan is described first as the 'fleeing serpent,' in Hebrew nachash bariach, and second as the 'coiling serpent,' nachash aqallaton. The BSB footnote notes that the word for serpent, nachash, is the same word used for the serpent of Genesis 3 and appears twice here. The first title is also found in Job 26:13, where God's hand 'pierced the fleeing serpent.' The third creature is the tannin, the dragon of the sea. The same word is used for the monster of Egypt, 'the great monster who lies among his rivers,' Ezekiel 29:3, and for what God pierced in Isaiah 51:9. The Bible keeps the same family of monster words for chaos, for Egypt's pharaoh and for the old enemy, which is why the debate over referent is real.

The thorns and briers of verse 4 are the pair shamir and shayit. The same two words stand together in Isaiah 5:6, where they grow up on the abandoned vineyard. The pair appears again in Isaiah 7:23-25 as signs of a land gone to waste. In chapter 27 they stand for the opposition that a keeper of the vineyard would burn, but the very next verse offers them an alternative, and the pairing shows how the song is a deliberate reversal.

The anger in verse 4 is chemah, heat, a word for fury. 'I am not angry' sets this vineyard against the first one. And in verse 5 the stronghold in which the thorns may take refuge is maoz, the word used for the 'stronghold' in Isaiah 25:4. The man who lays claim to the LORD's maoz enters the fortress that the poor shelter in. The peace of that verse is stated twice, as in the doubled shalom of Isaiah 26:3.

Verse 7 is built from a repeated sound. The first question piles up forms of the root for striking, the noun for a blow and the verb to strike, so that the Hebrew beats like a drum, and the second question answers it with the root for killing. Verse 8 then uses a rare word that the BSB footnote glosses as 'measure by measure,' with the alternative that the verse describes driving her into exile. The sense is a limit, a measured blow.

Verse 9 uses the verb that gives kippur, atonement, and ties it to 'fruit.' The Hebrew for 'the full fruit of the removal of his sin' says that fruit is what the removal of sin produces. This links verse 9 to the vineyard of verses 2 to 6, and means that atonement is not an end in itself. It is what lets the vine bear.

In verse 11 God is Maker and Creator, and yet 'has no compassion.' The verb for compassion is from the root related to the womb, the same word God uses when He promises everlasting compassion in Isaiah 54:8. The absence of that tenderness for a people without understanding is therefore a very heavy phrase, because it withholds the very thing the prophet elsewhere promises Israel.

Finally, 'gathered' in verse 12 uses the verb for gleaning, to pick up what has been left in a field, and 'thresh' is the verb for beating out grain. The harvest language continues from the vineyard. The scattered are pictured as grain beaten from the husk and picked up one stalk at a time.

typology.type: The sword against Leviathan, the serpent whose head is crushed
typology.fulfillment: God crushed the heads of Leviathan in Psalm 74:13-14, and the first promise was that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head, Genesis 3:15. In Christ the scene is made concrete. Jesus says He saw Satan fall like lightning, Luke 10:18, and that the ruler of this world will be cast out, John 12:31. At the cross He disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:15, and Revelation names the dragon as the ancient serpent, Revelation 12:9, bound in 20:2 and finally thrown into the lake of fire, 20:10. The type is not yet complete. The adversary still prowls, 1 Peter 5:8, and Isaiah's 'in that day' still has a last act.

typology.type: The vineyard the LORD keeps, and the true vine
typology.fulfillment: The vineyard of Isaiah 5 failed, and the vineyard of Isaiah 27 is guarded day and night by the LORD Himself. Jesus draws the two together. In Matthew 21:33-43 He tells of tenants who kill the owner's son, and in John 15:1 He says 'I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard.' The Keeper of Isaiah 27 is the Father, and the vine that finally bears fruit is the Son, with believers as branches, John 15:5. The type falls short in that the Israel of Isaiah was a nation under a covenant that it broke, while the vine of John is a person who does not fail.

typology.type: The atonement that clears idols and gives fruit
typology.fulfillment: Verse 9 ties atonement to the removal of altars and idols, a purge that frees the vine to bear. The New Testament states the same logic in a personal key. Christ appeared 'to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself,' Hebrews 9:26, and Paul commends the Thessalonians who 'turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,' 1 Thessalonians 1:9. Paul also cites the verse in Romans 11:27 for the Deliverer who takes away sins. The type falls short in its means. In Isaiah the focus is on judgment and exile as the clearing process, while Christ's atonement is not paid by Israel's suffering but by His own.

typology.type: The great ram's horn and the gathering of the scattered
typology.fulfillment: A ram's horn gathers the perishing from Assyria and the exiles from Egypt to worship on the holy mountain. Jesus applies the trumpet to the end, sending His angels with a loud trumpet call to gather His elect from the four winds, Matthew 24:31. Paul speaks of the last trumpet at which the dead are raised, 1 Corinthians 15:52. John says Jesus died to gather the scattered children of God into one, John 11:52. The gathering is wider than Isaiah named: from every nation, not only from Israel's old exile. The type is still moving toward its last stage.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the serpent. The sword of the LORD falls on the serpent of the sea, and the Bible's first promise, Genesis 3:15, was that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head. The New Testament links the two. The Son of God shared our flesh and blood 'so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,' Hebrews 2:14. Jesus saw Satan fall, Luke 10:18, announced that the ruler of this world would be cast out, John 12:31, and at the cross disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:15. Revelation names the great dragon as 'that ancient serpent,' Revelation 12:9, which is Isaiah's Leviathan in one more form. Isaiah does not name the Messiah in verse 1, and it would be a mistake to say he does. The sword is the LORD's. What the New Testament does is show the LORD fighting in the person of the Son.

It leads to Christ through the vineyard. The keeper of the vineyard says He waters it continually and guards it night and day. In John 15:1 Jesus says His Father is 'the keeper of the vineyard' and that He Himself is the true vine. The vineyard Israel could not stay fruitful because she turned to idols, Hosea 10:1. The vine who is Christ does bear fruit, and the branches that remain in Him bear much fruit, John 15:5. He is also the one who stands in the parable as the son thrown out of the vineyard and killed, Matthew 21:39, and the one the builders rejected, which ties this chapter to the stone of Isaiah 28.

It leads to Christ through atonement. Verse 9 promises that guilt will be atoned for and that the fruit of the removal of sin will be a people with no idols left. Paul cites the verse when he describes the Deliverer who will come from Zion and remove godlessness from Jacob, Romans 11:26-27, and the writer of Hebrews says Christ appeared 'to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself,' Hebrews 9:26. What Israel's exile could only clear, He deals with at the root.

And it leads to Christ through the trumpet. The ram's horn of verse 13 gathers the lost into a place of worship. Caiaphas, unwittingly, prophesied that Jesus would die 'not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one,' John 11:51-52. Isaiah 19:23-25 has already imagined Egypt and Assyria worshiping alongside Israel, and Revelation 7:9 sees the gathered multitude. The Jubilee trumpet began on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 25:9, and the pairing of atonement in verse 9 with the horn in verse 13 is a sequence that the cross and its aftermath fulfil: sin is removed, and the gathering begins.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as warrior and gardener in the same breath, and the doctrine that comes from it is that His power and His care are not two moods but one character. The sword that falls on Leviathan is sharp, great and mighty, which is to say that no piece of evil sits beyond its reach. The sea monster is the stuff of nightmare in the ancient world, and one verse disposes of it. God is not locked in a struggle whose outcome is in doubt.

He is patient and attentive. He waters the vineyard continually and guards it night and day, verse 3. Psalm 121:4 puts the same truth in a line: the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. His watch is steady and personal, and it reaches the smallest plants.

He is slow to anger and quick to offer peace. 'I am not angry' sits beside a willingness to burn thorns, and then the offer comes: let them make peace with Me. Divine wrath is real and it is set against the rebellion that He opposes, but it is not the first or last word. The offer in verse 5 is as open as His anger is firm.

He is just in how He measures. Verses 7 and 8 insist that Israel was not struck as her oppressors were, and the whole chapter holds that God knows the difference between purifying a people and destroying them. His discipline is proportioned, and it has a goal: the removal of sin and the clearing of idols, verse 9.

He is also sober in judgment. Verse 11 speaks of a people without understanding, and says their Maker has no compassion on them. That is a sentence about those who persistently refuse. It reminds us that the God who gives compassion can withdraw its felt effect from those who will not listen.

He is the gatherer, who collects His people one by one, verse 12, and calls them with a great horn. For worship, the chapter gives a song that can be sung before anything is visible, 'Sing about a fruitful vineyard,' and a trumpet to look forward to, which is how worship lives in the interval.

crossReferences.note: The beloved's vineyard on a very fertile hill, carefully prepared, yielded sour grapes. Isaiah 27 takes up the same image and reverses the outcome. The first song ended with a wasteland, and the new one begins with a call to sing about a fruitful vineyard under the LORD's own keeping.

God's hand pierced the fleeing serpent. Job uses the same two words that Isaiah 27:1 uses for the first title of Leviathan, showing that the title belonged to an older tradition of praise. The creature that frightened people is again just something God deals with by His hand.

The psalmist, in a time of national disaster, recalls that God divided the sea, smashed the heads of the dragons and crushed the heads of Leviathan. Isaiah 27:1 is the promise that He will do again what He did. Together they show that Israel's trust rested on what God had done and would do.

God promised that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head. Isaiah 27:1 shows the same enemy, using serpent language twice, going down under God's sword. The prophecy keeps the first promise alive across the centuries and gives it a day: in that day.

John identifies the great dragon as the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. It is the New Testament's way of saying who Leviathan is. The language of Isaiah 27:1 and the vision of Revelation meet in a single enemy and a single defeat.

Paul says that at the cross Christ disarmed the powers and authorities and triumphed over them. This is the decisive blow behind the promise of Isaiah 27:1. The sword of the LORD is wielded in the death of His Son, and the victory is already won even while it waits to be shown.

Jesus says He is the true vine and His Father is the keeper of the vineyard. The words recall the keeper of Isaiah 27:3, who waters the vineyard and guards it. The failed vineyard of Israel gives way to the vine that cannot fail, and believers are branches who bear fruit by remaining in Him.

Jesus tells a parable of a vineyard rented to tenants who kill the owner's son. It draws on Isaiah 5 and shows what fruitfulness the owner expected. The vineyard of Isaiah 27 is the hope that the owner will finally have it, tended by Himself.

Paul joins two promises, that the Deliverer will come from Zion, and that God will take away sins, to explain how Israel will be saved. The second half draws on Isaiah 27:9, so this chapter is part of how the apostle understands God's faithfulness to Jacob.

God's covenant with Abram gave a land from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates. Isaiah 27:12 draws the same boundaries when it speaks of the LORD's harvest from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt. The gathering is a return to the whole of the promised land, as originally given.

The horn sounded on the Day of Atonement proclaimed liberty and a return to one's property and clan in the Jubilee year. Isaiah 27 places atonement in verse 9 and a great ram's horn in verse 13, so the chapter reads like a Jubilee: sin removed, then the scattered called home.

The Lord will extend His hand a second time to recover the remnant of His people from Assyria, Egypt and other places, gathering the exiles and the scattered. The same lands and the same gathering appear in Isaiah 27:12-13, tying the two promises into one picture of homecoming.

Jesus says the Son of Man will send His angels with a loud trumpet call to gather the elect from the four winds. The trumpet of Isaiah 27:13 is carried into the Gospel's account of the end, now widened from the exiles of Israel to the elect from the whole earth.

Christ has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself. This is the answer to the question left standing in Isaiah 27:9, how guilt is finally atoned for. The chapter promised the removal of sin, and Hebrews says by what means.

study.oneStory:
The chapter begins where the Bible begins, with a serpent. In Genesis 3 the serpent brought a lie, and in Genesis 3:15 God promised that his head would be crushed. Every later conflict in the story, from Pharaoh's court to the empires that carried Israel away, is a version of that conflict. Isaiah 27:1 states in one sentence what the whole Old Testament waits for: God Himself will take the sword and deal with the serpent in the sea. The monster of the deep that Genesis 1:21 says God created is the one who will be slain.

The vineyard answers the story of Eden. A garden was given to humans to keep, and they were driven from it. Israel was a second planting, brought out of Egypt and put in a land, Psalm 80:8-9, and she too was uprooted, Isaiah 5. Isaiah 27 says the story does not end with the uprooting. The LORD is the keeper of the vineyard, He guards it night and day, and one day Israel will 'take root,' 'bud and blossom' and 'fill the whole world with fruit,' verse 6. That last phrase recalls the first commission to be fruitful and fill the earth, and also the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed. The failure of Israel does not cancel the plan. It is the reason the plan is carried by God Himself.

After Isaiah the story runs through exile and return, and then to Christ. He fights the serpent at the cross, is the true vine, and does away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself. Paul says that the removal of sins promised in this very chapter is part of how all Israel will be saved, Romans 11:26-27. The church lives in the middle, where the dragon is already disarmed, Colossians 2:15, and yet still prowls, 1 Peter 5:8. Its calling is to sing about the vineyard before the fruit is visible.

The end of the Bible takes up each of the chapter's images. The ancient serpent is bound and thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:2 and 20:10. The vineyard bears its fruit in a people from every nation. The great trumpet sounds, and those who were perishing come from the ends of the earth to worship on the holy mountain. The Day of Atonement horn becomes the horn of Jubilee, and the exiles of the old story arrive at last at a home with no enemy left to threaten it.

quiz.q: What does the LORD do to Leviathan in verse 1?

options.text: He slays it with His sharp, great, and mighty sword.
options.note: Verse 1 states this directly and dramatically.

options.text: He tames it and keeps it as a pet.
options.note: The opposite; the LORD destroys Leviathan, not domesticates it.

options.text: He negotiates a truce with it.
options.note: Not described in the text; the LORD's action is decisive judgment, not negotiation.

options.text: He ignores it entirely.
options.note: The opposite of the text's emphasis on direct, decisive action against Leviathan.

quiz.q: How does the LORD describe His care for Israel as a vineyard, verses 2 to 3?

options.text: He waters it continually and guards it night and day so nothing can disturb it.
options.note: Verse 3 describes this constant, attentive care in exactly these terms.

options.text: He abandons it entirely to fend for itself.
options.note: The opposite; He describes continual, attentive care, not abandonment.

options.text: He waters it only once a year during festivals.
options.note: Not what the text describes; the care given is continual, not occasional.

options.text: He hires foreign workers to tend it instead of doing so Himself.
options.note: The text specifically says, I, the LORD, am its keeper, emphasizing His own direct involvement.

quiz.q: How does verse 7 distinguish Israel's discipline from her oppressors' judgment?

options.text: The LORD did not strike or kill Israel as He struck and killed her oppressors.
options.note: Verse 7 draws this explicit contrast between measured discipline and total destruction.

options.text: Israel was treated more harshly than her oppressors in every way.
options.note: The opposite; the verse shows Israel was treated less severely than her oppressors.

options.text: Both Israel and her oppressors received identical judgment.
options.note: The text specifically contrasts, not equates, their treatment.

options.text: Israel's oppressors were shown greater mercy than Israel.
options.note: The opposite; Israel receives the greater mercy of measured discipline rather than destruction.

quiz.q: What is the concrete evidence, according to verse 9, that Jacob's guilt has been atoned for?

options.text: The altar stones are crushed and no Asherah poles or incense altars remain standing.
options.note: Verse 9 ties atonement concretely to the actual removal of idolatry.

options.text: Israel builds a larger temple than before.
options.note: Not mentioned in this verse; the evidence given is the removal of idols, not temple size.

options.text: Israel's population grows to exceed all other nations.
options.note: Not the specific evidence given in verse 9.

options.text: Israel forms new alliances with foreign powers.
options.note: Unrelated to this verse's actual point, which concerns the removal of idolatry as proof of atonement.

quiz.q: What happens when the great ram's horn sounds in verse 13?

options.text: Exiles from Assyria and Egypt come forth and worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.
options.note: Verse 13 describes exactly this joyful gathering and worship.

options.text: It signals the final destruction of Jerusalem.
options.note: The opposite; it signals gathering and worship, not destruction.

options.text: It calls Israel's army to war against Egypt.
options.note: Not described; the horn calls exiles home to worship, not to war.

options.text: It marks the beginning of a new famine.
options.note: Unrelated to the text's actual content, which is a joyful ingathering for worship.

questions: The LORD promises to finally slay Leviathan, the ancient serpent. What areas of chaos, fear, or evil in your own life or the world do you need to remember are already under God's certain, coming judgment?

God describes Himself as a keeper who waters His vineyard continually and guards it night and day. Where have you felt distant from that kind of attentive care, and how does this image invite you to trust Him again?

Israel's exile was real discipline, yet distinct from the destruction visited on her oppressors. How do you distinguish, in your own life, between God's loving discipline and simple punishment or abandonment?

True atonement for Jacob's guilt showed itself in the actual removal of idols, not just a change in status. What idols in your own life would need to visibly go for your repentance to bear that same kind of fruit?

Scattered exiles from Assyria and Egypt are gathered by a single ram's horn to worship together. Where do you long to see scattered or estranged people, in your family, church, or community, gathered back into worship and unity?

translationNotes.note: The threefold description of Leviathan, fleeing serpent, coiling serpent, dragon of the sea, echoes ancient chaos-monster language used elsewhere of cosmic evil.
